items.abstract:
<jats:title>Summary</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    <jats:list>
                      <jats:list-item>
                        <jats:p>
                          The use of both linear and generalized linear mixed‐effects models (
                          <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">LMM</jats:styled-content>
                          s and
                          <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">GLMM</jats:styled-content>
                          s) has become popular not only in social and medical sciences, but also in biological sciences, especially in the field of ecology and evolution. Information criteria, such as Akaike Information Criterion (
                          <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">AIC</jats:styled-content>
                          ), are usually presented as model comparison tools for mixed‐effects models.
                        </jats:p>
                      </jats:list-item>
                      <jats:list-item>
                        <jats:p>
                          The presentation of ‘variance explained’ (
                          <jats:italic>R</jats:italic>
                          <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                          ) as a relevant summarizing statistic of mixed‐effects models, however, is rare, even though
                          <jats:italic>R</jats:italic>
                          <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                          is routinely reported for linear models (
                          <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">LM</jats:styled-content>
                          s) and also generalized linear models (
                          <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">GLM</jats:styled-content>
                          s).
                          <jats:italic>R</jats:italic>
                          <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                          has the extremely useful property of providing an absolute value for the goodness‐of‐fit of a model, which cannot be given by the information criteria. As a summary statistic that describes the amount of variance explained,
                          <jats:italic>R</jats:italic>
                          <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                          can also be a quantity of biological interest.
                        </jats:p>
                      </jats:list-item>
                      <jats:list-item>
                        <jats:p>
                          One reason for the under‐appreciation of
                          <jats:italic>R</jats:italic>
                          <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                          for mixed‐effects models lies in the fact that
                          <jats:italic>R</jats:italic>
                          <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                          can be defined in a number of ways. Furthermore, most definitions of
                          <jats:italic>R</jats:italic>
                          <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                          for mixed‐effects have theoretical problems (e.g. decreased or negative
                          <jats:italic>R</jats:italic>
                          <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                          values in larger models) and/or their use is hindered by practical difficulties (e.g. implementation).
                        </jats:p>
                      </jats:list-item>
                      <jats:list-item>
                        <jats:p>
                          Here, we make a case for the importance of reporting
                          <jats:italic>R</jats:italic>
                          <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                          for mixed‐effects models. We first provide the common definitions of
                          <jats:italic>R</jats:italic>
                          <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                          for
                          <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">LM</jats:styled-content>
                          s and
                          <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">GLM</jats:styled-content>
                          s and discuss the key problems associated with calculating
                          <jats:italic>R</jats:italic>
                          <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                          for mixed‐effects models. We then recommend a general and simple method for calculating two types of
                          <jats:italic>R</jats:italic>
                          <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                          (marginal and conditional
                          <jats:italic>R</jats:italic>
                          <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                          ) for both
                          <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">LMM</jats:styled-content>
                          s and
                          <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">GLMM</jats:styled-content>
                          s, which are less susceptible to common problems.
                        </jats:p>
                      </jats:list-item>
                      <jats:list-item>
                        <jats:p>
                          This method is illustrated by examples and can be widely employed by researchers in any fields of research, regardless of software packages used for fitting mixed‐effects models. The proposed method has the potential to facilitate the presentation of
                          <jats:italic>R</jats:italic>
                          <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                          for a wide range of circumstances.
                        </jats:p>
                      </jats:list-item>
                    </jats:list>
                  </jats:p>
title: A general and simple method for obtaining R 2 from generalized linear mixed‐effects models

items.abstract: <jats:p>Considerable evidence indicates that domain specific knowledge in the form of schemas is the primary factor distinguishing experts from novices in problem‐solving skill. Evidence that conventional problem‐solving activity is not effective in schema acquisition is also accumulating. It is suggested that a major reason for the ineffectiveness of problem solving as a learning device, is that the cognitive processes required by the two activities overlap insufficiently, and that conventional problem solving in the form of means‐ends analysis requires a relatively large amount of cognitive processing capacity which is consequently unavailable for schema acquisition. A computational model and experimental evidence provide support for this contention. Theoretical and practical implications are discussed.</jats:p>
title: Cognitive Load During Problem Solving: Effects on Learning
Illiquidity and stock returns: cross-section and time-series effects

items.abstract: <jats:p>For consumers, evaluation of a service firm often depends on evaluation of the “service encounter” or the period of time when the customer interacts directly with the firm. Knowledge of the factors that influence customer evaluations in service encounters is therefore critical, particularly at a time when general perceptions of service quality are declining. The author presents a model for understanding service encounter evaluation that synthesizes consumer satisfaction, services marketing, and attribution theories. A portion of the model is tested experimentally to assess the effects of physical surroundings and employee responses (explanations and offers to compensate) on attributions and satisfaction in a service failure context.</jats:p>
title: Evaluating Service Encounters: The Effects of Physical Surroundings and Employee Responses
